name: Sodium hyaluronate

lead: Sodium hyaluronate is the common salt form of hyaluronic acid, a water-binding molecule naturally present in skin and joints. In moisturisers and serums it gives a hydrated, dewy, plumper-looking surface where fine lines look softer.

It acts as a humectant that binds water at the skin surface; lower-molecular-weight versions are marketed as penetrating deeper. Most clinical research concerns joint injections and eye surgery rather than cosmetic creams.

paras: It is applied in serums and moisturisers, often under a cream to seal in moisture. The plumping effect on surface hydration is immediate and lasts while it is in use.
Topical use is generally described as well tolerated. Injectable forms (fillers) carry reported risks such as bruising, vascular occlusion and granulomas.

angle.text: Sodium hyaluronate is the salt form of hyaluronic acid found in most moisturisers and serums. It binds water at the skin surface so skin looks hydrated, plumper and smoother. Its strongest medical data come from injectables and surgery.

lead: Sodium hyaluronate is the sodium salt of hyaluronic acid (HA), a linear polysaccharide of repeating glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine units found in skin, joint fluid and the eye [1][2]. It is the form usually listed in moisturisers and serums, and it is also used in medical products such as joint injections and ophthalmic surgical viscoelastics.

In skincare it is described as a humectant that binds water; lower-molecular-weight versions are marketed as penetrating deeper [1]. Evidence cited for sodium hyaluronate in the medical literature comes mainly from injectable or surgical uses rather than cosmetic topicals.
infobox: Hyalgan, Supartz, Euflexxa, Monovisc, Orthovisc, Healon

paras: Sodium hyaluronate is added to creams and serums for hydration and is said by manufacturers to improve elasticity [1]. Cross-linked HA is also used in injectable dermal fillers, with effects lasting roughly 6 to 12 months [3].

Sodium hyaluronate products are used for knee osteoarthritis injections [4][5], as viscoelastic agents in cataract surgery [6][7], and as a submucosal lift in endoscopic resection [8][9]. Studies have also examined a sodium hyaluronate membrane for preventing postoperative abdominal adhesions [10].

With fillers, reported complications include pain, bruising, redness, itching, vascular occlusion and nerve or microvessel injury, and occasional granulomatous reactions [3]. A Grokipedia summary states hypersensitivity and infection are rare [1]. Topical use is generally described as well tolerated, though irritation and allergy are possible with any cosmetic ingredient.

Hyaluronic acid was isolated by Karl Meyer and John Palmer in 1934 [3]. Pharmacia developed the ophthalmic product Healon in the 1970s and 1980s [3]. A 1985 Science paper reported that HA degradation products induced angiogenesis [11], and a 1985 study measured sodium hyaluronate concentration and molecular weight in synovial fluid across arthropathies [2].

Most trials involve medical rather than cosmetic uses. A 1998 randomized trial of intra-articular sodium hyaluronate (Hyalgan) in knee osteoarthritis was reported by the Hyalgan Study Group [4], and a registered trial with 421 participants compared two brands for knee OA [5]. Registered trials also cover shoulder, ankle and hip osteoarthritis [12][13][14], tennis elbow [15], and cataract surgery viscoelastics [6][7]. A 2010 Lancet systematic review examined injections including hyaluronate for tendinopathy [16]. No trial of topical sodium hyaluronate for facial appearance was found in this source set.
